## TL;DR

Added a focused responsive regression pass for the Checks and Releases screens. Headless WebKit rendered 24 long check steps and 24 long release metadata rows at phone, tablet, and desktop widths. The new cases passed at 375, 768, and 1280 pixels. I also tightened wrapping and width constraints for long check names, command snippets, and release descriptions. The QA evidence and its limits are recorded in `docs/qa/2026-11-checks-releases-data-qa.md`.

## Work and rationale

The task calls out a gap in QA rather than a known single broken interaction: both screens need to remain usable with large real-looking datasets at three specific viewport widths. I read the task specification, found the page-specific Vue styles, and reviewed the repository's existing headless WebKit conventions. There were useful narrow-layout checks elsewhere, but no test assembled long data for Checks and Releases together.

I added a Node-environment Vitest file that launches Playwright's WebKit browser headlessly. It constructs a compact representative fragment using the actual page style blocks and the page classes for check rows, step names, command snippets, release distribution titles, and provider metadata. Each test renders 24 steps and 24 channel metadata records, with long identifiers and URLs. It checks that all rows remain in the DOM, page scroll width does not exceed the viewport, and the channel action stays within the viewport. It also verifies long step title wrapping. The viewport matrix is exactly 375, 768, and 1280 pixels.

The test includes a brief wait after constructing content to reflect the data-after-loading state, but it does not pretend to measure network latency. This is deterministic local UI evidence; it does not depend on external services, accounts, or a live repository server.

While reviewing the CSS, I found places where the existing layout relied on surrounding constraints rather than explicit long-content behavior. Check step titles now have `min-width: 0` and `overflow-wrap: anywhere`. The command code block has a maximum width of its containing row while retaining horizontal scrolling, preserving readable commands without widening the page. Release provider metadata's safe wrapping now applies beyond the narrow-screen media query, and the distribution description can break long package references.

I wrote a QA note at `docs/qa/2026-11-checks-releases-data-qa.md` describing the fixture, observed checks, the code adjustments, and what the run does not prove. This distinction matters: a static browser fixture is strong evidence for layout at specified widths, but it is not a claim about production data shape or live network timing.

## Approaches tried

I first searched existing UI tests for WebKit setup, viewport matrices, page structure, and loading fixtures. The repository already provides a useful pattern: `@playwright/test` WebKit can be launched headlessly inside a Node-environment Vitest test, and tests can skip if the browser binary is absent. I reused that pattern instead of creating a new browser harness or touching build/check configuration.

I then inspected the actual page markup and class rules rather than inventing unrelated generic cards. The fixture mirrors the important row structure and uses the same scoped style blocks, allowing browser layout to reveal whether those structures stay within the viewport. The chosen dataset emphasizes failure-prone material: long unbroken names, long command paths, repeated package references, and enough rows to make the page meaningfully list-heavy.

## Challenges and blockers

The pages have large Vue templates and styles, so I used the existing `repoos outline` guidance and targeted searches/ranges to find the content and responsive rules. The Releases screen mixes distribution, email, and release-cut sections; the responsive test deliberately concentrates on distribution metadata and the page action rather than trying to reimplement all API-dependent state in a synthetic browser document.

There is an important scope boundary in the evidence. The “slow data” scenario is represented by a deterministic delayed arrival in the test, not by a throttled production server or network profile. This avoids fabricating external timing results and keeps the regression repeatable. Existing component tests remain responsible for API loading and action behavior.

## Key learnings

Responsive layout can fail even when the main page shell fits: a single long check identifier or provider URL can force a nested flex child wider than the viewport. Explicit `min-width: 0` on the flexible content and safe word breaking on human-readable identifiers prevent that class of overflow. For command text, wrapping is not always desirable because it can obscure command fidelity; a bounded, horizontally scrollable code block preserves the command while containing the page.

The exact viewport matrix should live in a browser regression, not just a CSS source assertion. Checking row count and action geometry alongside total page width helps catch a page that technically fits only because the content or control disappeared. The evidence note also records the limits of synthetic fixtures so future readers can distinguish layout assurance from live latency QA.
